essays.question: Evaluate whether such a high market share for one company is in the consumer interest.

source.marksEvidence: Source filename explicitly states (20); screenshot uses question number 20 from a different numbering scheme.

sections.summary: Economies of scale may lower prices
sections.point: A high market share can benefit consumers through lower prices.
logic: Large sales and output increase the scale of input purchases
Suppliers may offer bulk-buying discounts
Lower input costs per unit reduce LRAC from C1 to C2
The firm can lower its price while maintaining a viable profit margin
If cost savings are passed on, consumers pay less and consumer surplus rises

/diagrams/monopoly-consumer-benefits-kaa.alt: Original LRAC diagram: output rises from Q1 to Q2 and average cost falls from C1 to C2.

sections.summary: Cost savings may raise profits instead
sections.point: However, a high market share may reduce the incentive to pass cost savings on to consumers.
logic: Greater market power reduces competitive pressure to cut prices
The firm may keep its price unchanged despite lower LRAC
Cost savings increase the profit margin instead
The gain in consumer welfare is limited

sections.point: The significance of the benefit depends on how much of the cost saving is passed on to consumers.
logic: A high proportion passed on through lower prices produces a larger gain in consumer surplus
A high proportion retained as profit leaves consumers with little benefit
The pass-through of savings therefore matters more than the cost reduction alone

sections.point: A high market share may benefit consumers through greater investment in product development.
logic: Strong brand loyalty and fewer close substitutes may make demand relatively price inelastic
Greater market power permits higher prices and supernormal profit
Retained profits provide funds for R&D
Successful R&D improves product quality and meets consumer needs more closely
Consumer utility increases

sections.point: However, unsuccessful R&D may raise costs without improving products.
logic: Substantial development spending may fail to produce a successful product
Costs rise without a genuine improvement in quality
If these costs are passed on, consumers face higher prices
Consumers pay more without receiving greater utility

sections.point: Consumer benefit depends more on the nature and success of innovation than on the amount spent on R&D.
logic: Innovation that meets consumer needs increases utility
High spending without meaningful product improvement offers little benefit
Sustained consumer gains therefore require successful innovation, not simply large R&D budgets

essays.question: Discuss the reasons why a few large firms dominate the food retailing industry but not the hairdressing industry.

sections.point: Economies of scale can allow a few large firms to dominate the food retailing industry.
logic: Large operations require substantial input purchases
Bulk-buying discounts reduce input costs per unit
Lower LRAC allows lower prices
More customers are attracted and market share grows
Smaller retailers struggle to compete and may exit because of low profitability
Market concentration increases

sections.point: However, diseconomies of scale may weaken the cost advantage of large firms.
logic: A larger, more complex organisation is harder to coordinate
Communication difficulties slow decisions and reduce managerial efficiency
LRAC rises, offsetting economies of scale
Smaller firms can compete and survive
Market concentration may remain lower

sections.point: Customer loyalty to individual service providers can prevent a few large firms from dominating personal-service markets.
logic: Customers value personalised service and an established relationship
If an employee starts an independent business, loyal customers may follow
The new business gains an existing customer base
Independent firms can enter and survive
Many small firms compete, keeping market concentration low

sections.point: However, large firms may retain customers by retaining the employees to whom those customers are loyal.
logic: Higher wages and better promotion opportunities encourage employees to stay
Customers remain with their preferred service providers within the firm
Large firms retain their customer base and can expand
Loyalty to individual employees does not necessarily prevent market concentration

essays.question: Discuss pricing and non-pricing strategies that e-bike manufacturers might use to increase sales.

source.filename: Pricing vs non-pricing strategies – effects on sales (14).docx

essays.essayTitle: Price and Non-Price Strategies: Effects on Sales

sections.point: A firm can increase sales by reducing its price.
logic: A lower price improves affordability and relative price competitiveness
More consumers are willing and able to buy
Some consumers switch from competing products
Quantity demanded rises, increasing units sold

sections.point: However, the effectiveness of price cutting depends on price elasticity of demand.
logic: If demand is price inelastic, a price cut causes a less than proportionate rise in quantity demanded
The increase in units sold may be small
Price cutting may therefore have only a limited effect on sales volume

sections.point: Improving product quality can increase sales through product differentiation.
logic: Better quality and design meet consumer preferences more closely
The product becomes more differentiated from competing alternatives
Consumers are more likely to choose the firm’s product
Brand loyalty strengthens and close substitutes become less attractive
Demand, the customer base and market share increase

sections.summary: R&D costs may offset sales gains
sections.point: However, improving quality may involve high R&D costs that limit the increase in sales.
logic: Product development requires substantial funding
Production costs rise
The firm may raise prices to protect profit margins
Affordability falls and quantity demanded may decrease
The sales gain from higher quality is partly offset

essays.question: Evaluate whether revenue maximisation is a more realistic business objective than profit maximisation for firms in the supermarket industry.
essays.essayTitle: Revenue Maximisation as a Realistic Objective

sections.point: Revenue maximisation may be a realistic objective because higher output can generate economies of scale.
logic: Moving from profit maximisation to revenue maximisation increases output from Qp to Qr
Larger input purchases may secure bulk-buying discounts
Lower input costs reduce LRAC
Lower prices raise quantity demanded and improve competitiveness
Sales revenue and market share can increase

/diagrams/revenue-maximisation-realistic.alt: Original diagram comparing profit maximisation at Qp and revenue maximisation at Qr, with prices Pp and Pr.

sections.summary: May only be a short-run strategy
sections.point: However, revenue maximisation may be a means of achieving profit maximisation in the long run.
logic: Expansion of market share strengthens market power
Greater price-making ability allows higher future prices
A higher price may increase the profit margin
Revenue maximisation may therefore be a strategy rather than the ultimate objective

sections.summary: Depends on the firm's market position
sections.point: The more realistic objective depends on the firm’s position in the market.
logic: While reducing LRAC and expanding market share, revenue maximisation may be more realistic
Once stronger market power is established, higher prices can raise profit margins
Profit maximisation may then become the more realistic long-run objective

sections.point: The divorce of ownership from control may make revenue maximisation more realistic for large firms.
logic: Shareholders own the firm, while managers control pricing and output
Bonuses, prestige and responsibility may increase with revenue or firm size
Managers prefer a higher output target
Output expands beyond the profit-maximising point where MR = MC
Total revenue is maximised where MR = 0

sections.point: However, shareholder pressure may constrain managers who sacrifice too much profit.
logic: Low profits leave insufficient funds for dividends
Shareholder dissatisfaction increases
Managers face pressure or the risk of losing their positions
They may give greater priority to profit to satisfy shareholders

sections.summary: Depends on satisfying shareholders' profit expectations
sections.point: The feasibility of revenue maximisation depends on whether it generates enough profit to satisfy shareholders.
logic: Sufficient profit allows managers to continue pursuing higher output and revenue
If profits fall too low, shareholder pressure increases
Profit maximisation becomes more realistic when this profit constraint is binding

essays.question: Evaluate why the objectives of small and medium-sized enterprises may differ from those of large enterprises.

source.filename: Business objectives - SME vs large gpt修改版.docx

essays.essayTitle: Business Objectives: SMEs vs Large Firms

sections.point: Owner-managed SMEs may pursue satisficing rather than profit or growth maximisation.
logic: Owners have direct control over business decisions
They may value work–life balance more than additional profit or market share
Expansion requires time and effort and reduces leisure
Owners choose an acceptable level of profit
The firm remains small because of the owner’s personal objectives

sections.point: However, ambitious entrepreneurs may prefer revenue or profit maximisation to satisficing.
logic: Owners may seek higher income, market share and business success
They are willing to invest in technology and expand operations
Growth and higher returns become more important than remaining small
An SME may therefore pursue maximisation objectives

sections.point: The objectives of an SME depend on the owner’s level of ambition.
logic: A strong preference for work–life balance favours satisficing
A willingness to invest and expand favours revenue or profit maximisation
Ownership structure alone does not determine the objective

sections.point: The separation of ownership and control may encourage managers of large firms to pursue revenue maximisation.
logic: Shareholders own the firm, but managers have discretion over pricing and output
Managerial rewards, prestige and status may rise with revenue or firm size
Managers prefer a higher output and revenue target
The firm produces where MR = 0
Total revenue is maximised

/diagrams/sme-large-business-objectives-.alt: Original revenue-maximisation diagram, showing output Q where MR = 0.
/diagrams/sme-large-business-objectives-.sourceLocation: Business objectives - SME vs large gpt修改版.docx · word/media/image2.png

sections.point: However, large firms may also pursue satisficing because managers must maintain satisfactory shareholder returns.
logic: Low profits reduce the funds available for dividends
Dissatisfied shareholders may pressure or replace managers
Managers must first earn a satisfactory level of profit
They can then pursue their own objectives
Large firms may therefore also satisfice, like SMEs

sections.summary: Depends on profit and managerial discretion
sections.point: The extent of managerial discretion depends on how much profit the business earns.
logic: Revenue maximisation can continue if profits satisfy shareholders
Falling profits and dividends increase shareholder pressure
Maintaining satisfactory profit becomes a constraint on managerial objectives
Satisficing may be more realistic when this constraint becomes important

essays.question: Evaluate the possible benefits of a demerger.

sections.point: A demerger can benefit firms by allowing greater specialisation.
logic: Separating non-core activities allows resources and expertise to focus on fewer markets
Management becomes more specialised and efficient
MC and AC fall from MC1 and AC1 to MC2 and AC2
Lower costs increase supernormal profit
In the original diagram, profit rises from P1BCD to P2EFG

/diagrams/demerger-benefits-kaa1.jpeg.alt: Original demerger diagram showing lower MC and AC and the change in supernormal profit from P1BCD to P2EFG.
/diagrams/demerger-benefits-kaa1.jpeg.sourceLocation: Demergers - benefits --2022.10 Q8 gpt修改版.docx · word/media/image2.jpeg

sections.point: However, a demerger may increase costs by duplicating previously shared resources.
logic: Independent firms each need management, marketing and administration
Additional employees and separate departments duplicate fixed costs
Labour and operating costs increase
Higher costs may offset the gains from specialisation

sections.summary: Compare specialisation savings with duplication costs
sections.point: The benefit to firms depends on whether specialisation savings exceed the additional costs of operating separately.
logic: Compare efficiency savings with duplicated labour and operating costs
If savings are larger, total costs fall and profits rise
If duplication costs dominate, the demerger may not benefit the firm

sections.point: A demerger may benefit consumers through lower prices and better product quality.
logic: Smaller independent firms may have less market power
Where competition increases, firms face greater pressure to attract consumers
Lower prices improve consumer welfare
Greater specialisation can also improve understanding of consumer needs
Better-targeted product development increases consumer utility

sections.summary: Inconvenience and reduced choice may result
sections.point: However, a demerger may reduce consumer utility by increasing inconvenience and limiting choice.
logic: Consumers may need to deal with several firms rather than one diversified supplier
Search costs and time spent purchasing increase
Some unprofitable product lines may be discontinued
Fewer choices and greater inconvenience reduce consumer utility

sections.summary: Depends on whether products remain available
sections.point: The effect on consumer choice depends on whether products are actually removed from the market.
logic: If divisions simply become independent firms, the same products can remain available
The loss of choice may therefore be small
If unprofitable product lines are discontinued, the range of products shrinks
The negative effect on consumer welfare is then greater

essays.question: Discuss the possible impact of a merger on workers and consumers.

source.marksEvidence: Screenshot labels the question (e); treated as the U3 Q7(e) 14-mark structure.

essays.contentNote: 原文仅包含 workers 的第一组论证；题目同时要求 consumers，第二组 KAA2 / EVA2 尚未提供。原文的权衡已并入 EVA1，保持 14 分结构。

sections.point: A merger may increase long-term job security for workers.
logic: Combined market share and sales increase the scale of operation
Economies of scale lower LRAC
Lower prices improve price competitiveness and attract customers
Sales revenue and profitability become more stable
A lower risk of business failure reduces the risk of large-scale job losses

sections.point: However, a merger may cause redundancies when the combined firm removes duplicated jobs.
logic: Overlapping management and administrative roles increase labour costs
The combined firm may lay off workers to reduce duplication
Short-run job losses can offset the gain in long-term security
The effect depends on the scale of subsequent expansion
If a larger workforce is needed, workers may be retained or redeployed, limiting redundancies

essays.question: Evaluate the benefits of growth by merger.

source.filename: Mergers - benefits of external growth --2022.5 Q8.docx

essays.essayTitle: Benefits of External Growth by Merger

sections.summary: Mergers can generate economies of scale
sections.point: A merger can benefit firms by generating economies of scale.
logic: Combining firms expands the potential customer base and access to markets
Higher demand supports greater output
Larger input purchases allow bulk-buying discounts
Input costs per unit fall, reducing LRAC from C1 to C2
If price is unchanged, profit margins and profits increase

/diagrams/external-growth-merger-benefit.alt: Original economies-of-scale diagram showing higher output and LRAC falling from C1 to C2.
/diagrams/external-growth-merger-benefit.sourceLocation: Mergers - benefits of external growth --2022.5 Q8.docx · word/media/image2.jpeg

sections.point: However, a merger may create diseconomies of scale if the organisation becomes too large.
logic: A larger organisation becomes more complex
Communication and coordination across departments and locations become harder
Decisions slow and managerial efficiency falls
Higher LRAC offsets economies of scale
Profit margins may decrease

sections.summary: Compare economies with diseconomies of scale
sections.point: The benefit to firms depends on whether economies of scale exceed diseconomies of scale.
logic: Compare input-cost savings with additional organisational costs
If savings exceed additional costs, profits increase
If diseconomies dominate, the merger may reduce profits

sections.point: A merger may benefit consumers by combining resources to improve product quality.
logic: Firms pool finance, research expertise and distribution networks
Complementary resources support more R&D
Innovation improves products and quality
Products meet consumer needs more closely
Consumer utility increases

sections.point: However, greater monopoly power may weaken incentives to innovate and improve efficiency.
logic: A larger market share can reduce competitive pressure
The firm has less need to improve products to retain customers
Product development may slow
Organisational slack may increase X-inefficiency

sections.point: The benefit to consumers depends on the degree of competition and contestability after the merger.
logic: Continued competitive pressure sustains incentives for R&D and quality improvements
Strong monopoly power with little competitive pressure weakens these incentives
Pooling resources provides greater benefits when firms remain under pressure to innovate

essays.question: Evaluate the disadvantages of an oligopolistic market for producers and consumers.
essays.contentNote: 原文只有 consumers 的第一组论证；题目还要求 producers，KAA2 / EVA2 / Weighing2 尚未提供。

sections.point: Collusion in an oligopoly may harm consumers by raising prices.
logic: A few dominant firms can coordinate their behaviour more easily
Firms may agree to restrict output and charge higher prices
Competition decreases
Consumers pay more and consume less
Consumer surplus and welfare fall

sections.point: However, aggressive competition between oligopolistic firms may benefit consumers.
logic: Firms cut prices to avoid losing market share
Rivals may respond with further price cuts
A price war allows consumers to buy at lower prices
Consumer surplus may increase

sections.point: The effect on consumers depends on whether firms collude or compete aggressively.
logic: Collusion with weak price competition sustains high prices and reduces consumer surplus
Repeated competitive price cuts instead lower prices and increase consumer surplus
Consumer harm is more likely when collusion is sustained

essays.question: Evaluate the likely disadvantages for a business operating in an oligopolistic market structure.

source.filename: Oligopoly - disadvantages to firms and game theory --2024.1 Q9 gpt修改版.docx

essays.essayTitle: Disadvantages to Firms and Game Theory

sections.point: Interdependence in an oligopoly may trigger a price war that reduces firms’ profits.
logic: Each firm considers how rivals will respond to a price change
If B maintains its price, A can raise its payoff from 10 to 15 by cutting
Once A cuts, B can improve its payoff from 5 to 7 by also cutting
The same incentive applies to A, so both firms cut prices
Both receive 7 rather than the 10 each would receive by maintaining prices
Individually rational decisions leave both firms worse off

matrix.caption: Payoffs: (A, B)
matrix.sourceLocation: Original Word table following KAA1; cell contents preserved.

sections.point: However, firms may end a price war when sustained price cuts offer little advantage.
logic: All major firms match the lower prices
No firm retains a price advantage and market shares change little
Profit margins remain lower
Firms have a mutual incentive to stop price competition
Prices may rise again, making the price war temporary

sections.summary: Depends on how long prices remain low
sections.point: The significance of a price war depends on whether low prices persist in the long run.
logic: Repeated price cuts keep margins low and make the disadvantage significant
If firms stop price competition and tacitly coordinate, prices may recover quickly
The duration of low prices determines the sustained loss of profit

sections.point: Non-price competition can impose high costs on firms in an oligopoly.
logic: Firms compete through advertising, R&D and product quality
Maintaining market share against large established rivals requires substantial spending
Production and marketing costs increase
If additional sales revenue does not cover the extra costs, profit falls

sections.point: However, successful non-price competition may increase profits through product differentiation.
logic: Better quality, advertising and branding strengthen brand loyalty
Fewer close substitutes make demand less price elastic
The firm can charge a higher price without losing many customers
If extra revenue exceeds extra cost, profit increases

sections.summary: Compare additional revenue with additional costs
sections.point: The net effect of non-price competition depends on whether additional revenue exceeds additional cost.
logic: Expensive advertising and R&D with little demand growth reduce profits
Strong brand loyalty and higher pricing power can generate larger revenue gains
Non-price competition is a disadvantage only when its costs outweigh these gains

essays.question: Discuss reasons why many SMEs shut down.

sections.point: A fall in revenue may cause a firm to shut down in the short run if it can no longer cover variable costs.
logic: Weaker demand may reduce the price and average revenue the firm receives
If AR falls below AVC, total revenue is insufficient to cover variable costs
Continued production increases losses relative to shutting down
The firm shuts down in the short run below P2 in the original diagram
Between P2 and P1, it can still contribute towards fixed costs and continue operating

/diagrams/sme-shutdown-reasons-kaa1.jpeg.alt: Original shutdown diagram showing MC, AC and AVC, with P1 at minimum AC and P2 at minimum AVC.

sections.summary: Revenue may remain above shutdown level
sections.point: However, not all firms experience a large enough fall in revenue to reach the shutdown point.
logic: Some goods and services remain essential when demand elsewhere weakens
Demand and revenue for these firms may remain stable or increase
AR can remain above AVC
Variable costs are covered, allowing the firm to continue operating

sections.summary: Rising variable costs may force shutdown
sections.point: Rising variable costs may force a firm to shut down in the short run.
logic: Higher input or operating costs increase AVC
AVC may rise above the average revenue received
Total revenue no longer covers variable costs
Continuing production would add to losses relative to shutting down
The firm ceases production

sections.point: However, government support that reduces variable costs may allow a firm to continue operating.
logic: A subsidy can reduce the variable cost borne by the firm
AVC may fall below AR
Revenue once again covers variable costs and contributes towards fixed costs
The firm can continue producing

essays.essayTitle: Non-price Competition: Benefits to Consumers and Businesses
essays.question: Discuss the benefits of non-price competition for consumers and businesses.

sections.point: Non-price competition can benefit consumers through higher-quality products.
logic: Firms invest more in R&D
R&D can lead to innovation and product differentiation
Product features and quality improve
Products better meet consumers' needs and preferences
Consumers gain greater choice and utility
Consumer welfare increases

sections.point: However, these benefits depend on whether R&D leads to successful innovation.
logic: Large firms may already have significant market power
Weaker competitive pressure can reduce the incentive to reinvest profits in R&D
Even when firms invest, R&D is risky and may fail
Costs may rise without genuine product improvements
Consumer utility may not increase significantly
The benefit to consumers may therefore be limited

sections.point: Advertising and branding may increase sales and profits for businesses.
logic: Advertising increases consumer awareness and familiarity
Brand loyalty becomes stronger
Consumers become less willing to switch to rivals
Demand becomes more price-inelastic
The firm can charge a higher price without losing many customers
Revenue and profit can increase
The firm may gain or protect market share

sections.point: However, non-price competition may reduce profits if its additional costs are too high.
logic: Advertising and other non-price strategies increase firms' costs
Rivals may respond with more advertising, creating an advertising race
The increase in costs may exceed the additional revenue generated
Profit margins may fall
The benefit may also be temporary if consumers switch to better rival products
Profits rise significantly only when additional revenue and long-term brand loyalty outweigh the additional cost

essays.essayTitle: Shutdown Decision: Normal Profit and Costs
essays.question: Evaluate the view that a business will always shut down if it is not able to make a normal profit.

sections.point: If a firm cannot cover its total costs in the long run, it is likely to shut down.
logic: Failure to make normal profit means AR is below AC
Total revenue is below total cost, so the firm makes a loss
Persistent losses reduce financial reserves
The firm becomes less able to pay workers, suppliers and other costs
In the long run, all costs are variable
The firm must cover total costs including opportunity cost to remain in the market
Persistent AR below AC makes continued operation unsustainable
Shutdown becomes increasingly likely

sections.point: However, failing to make normal profit does not necessarily mean the firm should shut down immediately.
logic: The loss may only be temporary
A temporary fall in demand can push AR below AC
Demand may later recover
AR may rise and the firm may return to normal profit
Shutdown can also create exit costs and make later re-entry difficult
The firm may therefore remain open if managers expect conditions to recover

sections.summary: Duration of losses and financial position
sections.point: The shutdown decision depends on whether the loss is temporary or persistent and whether the firm has enough finance to survive it.
logic: Strong cash reserves or access to credit allow the firm to tolerate losses for longer
This gives the firm time to wait for demand to recover
Weak liquidity may force the firm to close even if future conditions are expected to improve
The duration of the loss and the firm's financial position therefore affect the shutdown decision

sections.summary: AR above AVC supports continued production
sections.point: In the short run, a firm may continue operating even if it cannot make normal profit.
logic: AR can be below AC while remaining above AVC
The firm makes a loss but revenue still covers all variable costs
Revenue also makes a contribution towards fixed costs
If the firm shuts down, revenue falls to zero while fixed costs remain
The firm would lose its contribution towards fixed costs
Continuing production therefore minimises the firm's loss
The firm should remain open in the short run while AR is above AVC

/diagrams/shutdown-normal-profit-kaa2.jp.alt: Short-run shutdown diagram showing MC, AC and AVC with P1 and P2.
/diagrams/shutdown-normal-profit-kaa2.jp.caption: Short-run shutdown decision: a loss-making firm can continue while AR remains above AVC.

sections.point: However, if AR falls below AVC, shutting down is the loss-minimising decision.
logic: Revenue is not enough to cover the variable costs of production
Continued production adds more to variable cost than it generates in revenue
Each additional unit therefore increases the firm's total loss
Shutdown allows the firm to avoid variable costs
Fixed costs still remain in the short run
Once AR falls below AVC, shutdown minimises losses

sections.point: The short-run shutdown rule is important, but the firm's objectives, expectations and financial position can affect how long it continues operating.
logic: A firm may prioritise survival or long-term growth over short-run profit
It may accept losses while establishing a customer base or waiting for demand to recover
This strategy is sustainable only if the firm has enough finance to fund the losses
The final shutdown decision therefore depends on both the cost condition and the firm's ability and willingness to continue
